title: Plato’s Cave
subtitle: Shadows, light and where you stand
learning_objective: Tell apart what you see from what makes you believe it: shadows depend on a light, an object and where you stand. Connect this to Plato’s distinction between opinion and knowledge.
disclaimer: A teaching version of a philosophical allegory — it is not a scientific experiment about perception and does not prove Plato’s theory of Forms.

steps.title: Observe
steps.prompt: You are chained facing a wall. Shapes move across it. This is all you have ever seen.

steps.title: Judge
steps.prompt: What is the shape moving on the wall?

steps.title: Experiment
steps.prompt: Move the fire, move the object, turn around, go outside. Watch what happens to the shadow.

steps.title: Judge again
steps.prompt: Could the shadow alone tell you what the horse is really like?

steps.title: Explain
steps.prompt: Three ways to read what you saw.

steps.title: Apply
steps.prompt: Find a ‘shadow’ in your own life.

steps.title: Keep
steps.prompt: Keep what you understood and what you still wonder about.

feedback_rules.say: To you, these shapes are simply the world. You have nothing else to compare them with.
That is what anyone in the chains would say. Keep it — next, look at what makes the shape.
You already suspect there is more behind the wall. Let’s find out what.
Not sure is fair — you have only ever seen the wall.
Move the light and the same object casts a different shadow — higher, lower, stretched.
Closer to the fire, the shadow grows; closer to the wall, it shrinks. The object itself did not change size.
Turned around, you see the fire and the carved figures. The ‘horse’ was a puppet — the shadow of a copy.
Outside, in daylight, you see a real horse. In the allegory this stands for understanding what things truly are.
Back facing the wall: the shadows look exactly as before — but now you know what makes them.
Right — the shadow depends on the light, the puppet and your position. It can’t show what a horse is.
Partly: the outline carries some information, but you couldn’t know which parts — without leaving the chains.
Think back: the same puppet gave tall, short and stretched shadows. Which one is ‘the horse’?

layers.title: ① What the allegory shows
layers.body: Prisoners who have only seen shadows take them for reality. One is freed, turns to the fire, climbs out and finally sees things in sunlight. Returning, he is not believed.
layers.source: Plato, Republic VII, 514a–520a — check the line numbers against your edition
layers.maps_to: The wall · turning around · going outside

layers.title: ② Opinion and knowledge
layers.body: Plato separates opinion (about appearances) from knowledge (of what things truly are, which he calls Forms). The Divided Line in Republic VI orders these levels: images, things, then mathematics and the Forms. The ascent from the cave is often read alongside it, and the sun stands for the Form of the Good.
layers.maps_to: From ‘what I see’ to ‘why I believe it’

layers.title: ③ What it is not
layers.body: The cave is a philosophical allegory about knowledge and education, not a scientific account of vision. Plato’s theory of Forms is one position; many philosophers reject it. The experiment helps you ask “what makes me believe this?” — it does not show that Forms exist.
layers.source: See e.g. Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, “Plato” and “Plato’s Middle Period Metaphysics and Epistemology”

content.map_note: Keep two questions apart: what did I see? — and why do I believe it?
